entities.name: Angers Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cathedral of Saint Maurice in Angers, France, rebuilt in the 12th-13th centuries in Angevin Gothic style — the distinctive architectural school developed in Anjou (the Plantagenet dynasty's home county) — is one of the most important examples of early Gothic architecture outside Île-de-France, notable for its extraordinarily wide nave (16.48 meters, among the widest Gothic naves in France) achieved through Angevin vault technique ('domed' ribbed vaults with a single bay covering very large areas rather than the Parisian two-bay system). The cathedral's Plantagenet connection makes it a center of English royal history.

Anjevine Gothic (also called Plantagenet Gothic after the dynasty) was developed in the Loire Valley in the 12th century as an alternative to the Île-de-France Gothic pioneered at Saint-Denis and Notre-Dame de Paris. The Angevin vault — higher, domed, with a single bay spanning 16+ meters — was technically distinct from Parisian Gothic. Angers Cathedral's nave (rebuilt 1149-1240 CE) is the masterwork of this regional style. Geoffrey V of Anjou (d. 1151, father of Henry II of England) commissioned the earliest phases.

Angers is the capital of Anjou — the Plantagenet dynasty's ancestral county — making the cathedral the spiritual center of the dynasty that ruled England (1154-1485, Henry II through Richard III) and controlled territories from Scotland to the Pyrenees. The cathedral's 12th-century tapestry collection (Notre-Dame de Nantilly) is one of France's most important medieval textile holdings. The Apocalypse Tapestry (1377-1382, commissioned by Louis I of Anjou) — the world's largest surviving medieval tapestry series, 140 meters long — is housed in Angers Castle nearby.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Angers Cathedral — ancestral spiritual center of the Plantagenet dynasty that ruled England for 331 years, masterwork of Angevin Gothic's wide-bay vault innovation, and adjacent to the world's largest surviving medieval tapestry — is one of the most historically dense provincial French cathedrals, connecting English royal history to architectural innovation.
